newsitem.title: USA: Mrs. Clinton hopes Africa trip will pay dividends.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton hopes Africa trip will pay dividends.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton returned on Sunday from a two-week tour of six African countries hoping she generated interest in Africa among Americans and helped create a climate for increased U.S. investment there.

Her trip laid the foundation for a similar tour by U.S. President Bill Clinton during his second four-year term. Aides said it was unclear when that trip would take place but that there was a window of opportunity for it early next year.

U.S. officials travelling with the first lady said it was hoped that her trip would generate some enthusiasm in Congress for a new Africa policy that will promote increased trade and investment with the sub-Saharan region.

Mrs. Clinton, in a speech wrapping up her trip on Friday night in Kampala, Uganda, said she believed she had underscored during her "remarkable" journey that African and Americans must stand together.

"As I prepare to return home, it is with the hope that this trip may reflect the growing consciousness in the minds of the people of Africa and America that, despite the wide ocean between us, we are neighbours on this shared Earth," she said. "In our relationship, there must no longer be an 'us,' or a 'them,' but only a 'we.'"

A senior U.S. official travelling with the first lady said Africa will undoubtedly grow in importance for the United States because America is increasingly relying on African oil for its petroleum needs. Africa at this point is serving 15 percent of America's petroleum market.

With a Republican Congress looking for ways to cut foreign aid, compromise legislation on a new Africa policy might include combining traditional developmental assistance with increased opportunities for American companies to invest in Africa.
The senior official said this could involve granting preferential treatment to certain African exports in exchange for African governments allowing more U.S. investment.
Policymakers see the time as ripe for such a move because America is respected more in Africa than the former colonial powers, Britain, France and Portugal.

"We don't come with that baggage of having been a colonial power in Africa," the official said. Of the French in particular, who consider themselves a major power in Africa, this official said: "They know that Africa is too big and African problems too big to try to solve them on ther own."
During her trip, Mrs. Clinton visited Senegal in West Africa, travelled to South Africa, then Zimbabwe in southern Africa and then Tanzania, Uganda and Eritrea in East Africa.
She combined daily events and speeches to press her point that there is some good news about African progress beyond the daily headlines about refugee crises and fighting in Zaire.

She spread goodwill wherever she went, like giving a U.S.-purchased solar panel to the electricity-deprived Saam Njaay village in Senegal, announcing an $8 million grant to Uganda's education, or promising to find sewing machines for entrepreneurial women in a Zimbabwean village.

She pressed the point that only by pursuing democracy and free markets can African countries rebound from past policies that left many of their economies shattered and the people in poverty. She insisted that women be given equal rights and that children have proper education and health care.
And she managed to avoid any questions about the Democratic fund-raising scandal that has consumed Washington in recent weeks.
The trip also provided a new look at the Clintons' 17-year-old daughter, Chelsea. During a stop in Tanzania, Mrs. Clinton told a group of schoolgirls they should ask Chelsea some questions.
Chelsea went on to say that many American youth are troubled by drugs and violence and that the youth themselves will have to solve the problem because adults can only do so much.

Mrs. Clinton later regretted that she had put her protected daughter in the position of talking before reporters, but Chelsea's peformance showed her to be learned and mature and her message no different than that of her parents.
